memories.content: Use a flow diagram rather than a sequence table when alternate procedural branches lead to different outcomes.
Draw alternate branches and their resulting outcomes in the same flow diagram so readers can compare them at once.
The visual fidelity of a prototype may differ from its functional fidelity.
A flow diagram can make alternate branches and their different outcomes visible in one view.
HCI reviewers often skim prototype screens and interaction flow diagrams before reading the main text.
Readers can understand the overall branching shape of a procedure more quickly from a flow diagram than from rows read one at a time.
Redrawing a branching flow diagram after a procedural change usually takes longer than updating one row in a table.
Reviewers often inspect the proposal’s main visual before reading the procedural explanation in full.
Use an em dash only for a deliberate interruption or sharp contrast; otherwise split the sentence or choose ordinary punctuation.
In procedural passages, begin each sentence with the action, condition, or output instead of repeating “we” so the steps remain easy to follow and reuse.
Write system behaviors confirmed in the actual usage environment as observed states.
Write system behaviors not yet confirmed in the field as conditional plans.
Readers can reconstruct a sequence more accurately when each sentence begins with the action or condition rather than the author.
Do not mechanically split connected thoughts into separate short sentences when doing so destroys the intended reading rhythm.
Preserve a longer sentence when its clauses form one continuous movement that is easier to follow together than apart.
The user understands that short sentences are easier to scan but feels that uniformly segmented prose loses its reading rhythm.
Write procedural sentences so their opening phrase can be reused as a checklist item without changing the step's meaning.
The user should choose “I” as an individual author or “we” for a named team and should not mix them when describing the same responsible party.
Action-first procedural sentences can be reordered or copied into a checklist more easily because their subject is the step rather than the proposal author.
The user can explain whether an em dash marks an intentional interruption or contrast rather than using it decoratively.
An em dash creates a stronger interruption than a comma and can make a deliberate contrast easier to hear in the sentence.

analysis.overview: The frames address different presentation layers without directly overlapping: REFERENCE focuses on choosing and maintaining procedural visuals and anticipating reviewer behavior, while COMPARED sets prose conventions for procedural clarity, evidential certainty, sentence rhythm, pronouns, and em-dash use.

relations.reason: These memories jointly state and explain one REFERENCE-only recommendation about representing branching procedures visually.
relations.summary: Flow diagrams should present alternate procedural branches and outcomes together because they reveal branching structure more readily than sequential table rows.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful REFERENCE-only distinction about dimensions of prototype fidelity.
relations.summary: A prototype’s visual fidelity and functional fidelity may differ.

relations.reason: These memories restate one REFERENCE-only observation about reviewers’ visual-first reading behavior.
relations.summary: Reviewers often inspect a proposal’s principal visuals, including prototype screens and interaction-flow diagrams, before reading its full explanation.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful REFERENCE-only maintenance tradeoff.
relations.summary: After a procedural change, revising a branching flow diagram usually requires more effort than updating a table row.

relations.reason: These memories state the COMPARED-only usage rule, its communicative effect, and the corresponding test of authorial intent.
relations.summary: An em dash should mark an intentional strong interruption or sharp contrast rather than serve as decorative punctuation.

relations.reason: These memories state and explain one COMPARED-only action-first convention for procedural writing.
relations.summary: Procedural sentences should begin with the action, condition, or output so their steps are easy to follow, reorder, and reuse as checklist items.

relations.reason: The two memories split one COMPARED-only policy for matching behavioral claims to available evidence.
relations.summary: Descriptions of system behavior should reflect confirmation status: field-confirmed behavior is written as observed, while unconfirmed behavior is written as a conditional plan.

relations.reason: These memories express one COMPARED-only preference against uniformly segmented prose and explain its readability basis.
relations.summary: Connected thoughts should remain in a longer sentence when splitting them would harm continuity or intended reading rhythm.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful COMPARED-only rule for consistent attribution.
relations.summary: Authorship should use “I” for an individual or “we” for a named team without mixing them for the same responsible party.

reports.compared_only: COMPARED covers purposeful em dashes, action-first reusable steps, evidence-sensitive behavior claims, connected sentence rhythm, and consistent authorial pronouns.
reports.reference_only: REFERENCE favors flow diagrams for branching procedures, distinguishes prototype fidelities, notes visual-first review behavior, and recognizes diagram maintenance cost.
